q: In physics, work is done only when an object moves under the influence of a force.
e: This is the exact definition of work provided in the textbook.

q: Work may be defined as the scalar product of the force applied and the displacement.
e: The textbook explicitly defines work as the scalar product of force and displacement.

q: The work by a force is given by the equation $W = Fs \cos \theta$.
e: This is the correct mathematical representation of work done by a force at an angle.

q: The change in potential energy is equal to the work done on the object.
e: The textbook states that work is equal to the change in energy, specifically potential energy in this context.

q: The rate of doing work is defined as power.
e: This is the fundamental definition of power in physics.

q: The unit for power in SI units is the watt (W).
e: The watt is the standard SI unit for measuring power.

q: If the work done is 1 joule in 1 second, the power is 1 watt.
e: This is the exact definition of 1 watt as stated in the textbook.

q: The units of power which are larger than watt are kilowatt (kW) and megawatt (MW).
e: Kilowatt and megawatt are explicitly listed as larger units of power.

q: $1 \text{ kW} = 1000 \text{ W} = 10^3 \text{ W}$.
e: This is the correct conversion for kilowatts to watts as provided in the text.
This is the correct conversion for megawatts to watts as provided in the text.

q: In the CGS system, the unit of power is erg s$^{-1}$.
e: The textbook specifies erg s$^{-1}$ as the CGS unit for power.

q: In the British system, the unit of power is foot-pound per second (ft-lb s$^{-1}$).
e: Foot-pound per second is correctly identified as the British system unit for power.

q: In the British engineering system, the unit of power is horse power (hp).
e: Horse power is the specified unit for power in the British engineering system.

q: If the work done in 1 second is 550 ft-lb, the power is 1 horse power.
e: This is the exact definition of 1 horse power provided in the textbook.
This is the correct relationship between watts, joules per second, and ergs per second.

q: $1 \text{ hp} = 550 \text{ ft-lb s}^{-1} = 746 \text{ W}$.
e: This is the correct conversion for horse power to watts and ft-lb s$^{-1}$.

q: Power is equal to the product of force and velocity ($P = Fv$).
e: The textbook derives and states that power is the product of force and average velocity.

q: Power is a fundamental concept of physics.
e: Power is not a fundamental concept of physics, although it is a very important concept for engineering works.

q: Car engines, water pumps, refrigerators, air conditioners and electric bulbs are specified according to their power consumption.
e: The textbook lists these specific devices as examples of things specified by power consumption.

q: $1 \text{ kW} = 10^6 \text{ W}$.
e: 1 kW is equal to $10^3$ W, not $10^6$ W (which is 1 MW).

q: $1 \text{ hp} = 750 \text{ W}$.
e: 1 hp is exactly equal to 746 W, not 750 W.

q: In the British system, the unit of power is the joule per second.
e: In the British system, the unit of power is foot-pound per second (ft-lb s$^{-1}$).

q: Power is equal to the product of mass and velocity.
e: Power is equal to the product of force and velocity ($P = Fv$), not mass and velocity.

q: The rate of energy change is also important in practice.
e: The textbook explicitly states that the rate of energy change is important in practice.

q: If $s$ is the displacement produced by a constant force $F$ acting for the time $t$, the work done is $Fs$.
e: This is the correct formula for work done by a constant force in the direction of displacement.

q: For uniform motion, velocity $v$ is constant, so $P = Fv$.
e: The textbook confirms that for uniform motion, the power equation simplifies to $P = Fv$.

q: In the CGS system, if the work done is 1 erg in 1 second, the power is 1 erg s$^{-1}$.
e: This is the exact definition of the CGS unit of power as stated in the text.

q: $1 \text{ hp} = 746 \times 10^7 \text{ erg s}^{-1}$.
e: This is the correct conversion of horse power to ergs per second as provided in the textbook.

q: Efficiency is a technical term that is derived from everyday usage.
e: The textbook explicitly states that efficiency is derived from everyday usage.

q: In physics and engineering, efficiency has a precise meaning.
e: Unlike everyday usage, efficiency has a precise, technical meaning in physics and engineering.

q: The term efficiency is used in association with machines and devices.
e: The textbook specifies that efficiency is associated with machines and devices.

q: A simple machine is a mechanical device that amplifies the magnitude of a force and changes its position.
e: This is the exact definition of a simple machine provided in the text.

q: Simple machines are used to make work easier.
e: The textbook states that the purpose of simple machines is to make work easier.

q: Nowadays, machines are just combinations or more complicated forms of the six simple machines.
e: Modern machines are described as combinations or complex forms of the six simple machines.

q: The six simple machines are lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, screw and wedge.
e: These are the exact six simple machines listed in the textbook.

q: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of effort to load.
e: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of load to effort ($MA = L / E$), not effort to load.

q: Mechanical advantage is defined as $MA = L / E$.
e: This is the correct formula for mechanical advantage as stated in the textbook.

q: In practice, friction is always present in a machine.
e: The textbook notes that friction is always present, meaning some effort is spent overcoming it.

q: Because of friction, the small effort applied will have to move through a big distance to lift a large load.
e: This is a direct consequence of friction and the conservation of energy in machines.

q: The ratio of the distance moved by the effort to that of the load in the same time is called the velocity ratio of the machine.
e: This is the exact definition of velocity ratio provided in the textbook.

q: Velocity ratio is defined as $VR = s_{\text{load}} / s_{\text{effort}}$.
e: Velocity ratio is defined as $VR = s_{\text{effort}} / s_{\text{load}}$, not the inverse.

q: The velocity ratio of a machine is usually much greater than 1.
e: The textbook explicitly states that the velocity ratio of a machine is usually much greater than 1.

q: In lifting a load with a machine, work done on the load is called the output work.
e: The work obtained by lifting the load is correctly defined as output work.

q: Work done by the effort during the same time interval is called the input work.
e: The work supplied by the effort is correctly defined as input work.

q: The ratio of output work to input work is defined as the efficiency of the machine.
e: This is the precise definition of efficiency for a machine.

q: Efficiency is generally expressed in the percentage form.
e: The textbook states that efficiency is generally expressed as a percentage.

q: Efficiency is related to MA and VR as $\text{efficiency} = (MA / VR) \times 100\%$.
e: This is the correct mathematical relationship between efficiency, mechanical advantage, and velocity ratio.

q: It is possible, in practice, to build a perfect machine for which output work is equal to input work.
e: It is impossible in practice to build a perfect machine; input work always exceeds output work due to friction.

q: Input work always exceeds output work.
e: Because some work is always lost to friction, input work must be greater than output work.

q: The efficiency of a machine must always be less than 100%.
e: Since input work always exceeds output work, efficiency can never reach 100%.

q: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of the distance moved by the load to the distance moved by the effort.
e: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of load to effort ($L/E$). The ratio of distances relates to velocity ratio.

q: If a small load is attached to the free end of a suspended spring, the spring will be stretched or elongated.
e: This describes the basic elastic behavior of a spring under a load.

q: When the load is taken off, the spring will return to its original length and form.
e: This is the defining characteristic of elastic behavior within the elastic limit.

q: Ability to retain the original form when the applied force is removed is called elasticity.
e: This is the exact definition of elasticity provided in the textbook.

q: Not only springs but also other objects such as threads and rubber bands have elastic property.
e: The textbook explicitly lists threads and rubber bands as other objects with elastic properties.

q: Elastic limit is a limit, beyond which if an elastic object is stretched, it will return to its original form.
e: Beyond the elastic limit, the object will NOT return to its original form.

q: The elastic limit is different for different elastic bodies.
e: The textbook states that the elastic limit varies depending on the elastic body.

q: Robert Hooke noted that the amount of elongation of the spring is proportional to the applied force that produces it so long as the elastic limit is not exceeded.
e: This is the foundational observation of Hooke's Law as described in the text.

q: The amount of elongation is also called extension.
e: The textbook explicitly states that elongation is also referred to as extension.

q: Hooke's law is formally stated as: As long as the elastic limit of a body is not exceeded, the strain produced is proportional to stress causing it.
e: This is the exact formal statement of Hooke's Law provided in the textbook.

q: In symbols, Hooke's law is $F \propto x$ or $F = kx$.
e: This is the correct mathematical representation of Hooke's Law.

q: In Hooke's law, $F$ is the applied force or stress.
e: The textbook defines $F$ as the applied force, which corresponds to stress in this context.

q: In Hooke's law, $x$ is the elongation or strain.
e: The textbook defines $x$ as the elongation, which corresponds to strain in this context.

q: In Hooke's law, $k$ is a constant called the spring constant.
e: The constant of proportionality $k$ is specifically named the spring constant for a spring.

q: The unit of the spring constant $k$ is N m$^{-1}$.
e: The textbook explicitly states that the unit of $k$ is N m$^{-1}$.

q: Hooke's law expresses the elastic behavior of materials.
e: The textbook states that Hooke's law expresses the elastic behavior of materials.

q: The directly proportional relationship between applied force and elongation is expressed graphically by a straight line.
e: A directly proportional relationship always graphs as a straight line through the origin.

q: If a spring is compressed or stretched to an extension $x$, work is done by the applied force.
e: Work is done by the applied force to compress or stretch the spring.

q: This work done is stored as the potential energy of the spring.
e: The textbook states that the work done is stored as the elastic potential energy of the spring.

q: The work done is given by the area under the curve of the force-extension graph.
e: The textbook explains that the work done is represented by the area under the force-extension graph.

q: The elastic potential energy stored by the stretched spring is $PE = \frac{1}{2} kx^2$.
e: This is the correct formula for the elastic potential energy of a spring.

q: The unit of the spring constant $k$ is N m.
e: The unit of the spring constant $k$ is N m$^{-1}$, not N m.

q: The relationship between applied force and elongation is expressed graphically by a curved line.
e: The directly proportional relationship is expressed graphically by a straight line, not a curved line.

q: The elastic limit is the same for all elastic bodies.
e: The textbook explicitly states that the elastic limit is different for different elastic bodies.

q: Energy is the ability to do work or the total power derived from the natural resources we use.
e: This is the exact definition of energy provided in the textbook.

q: Energy exists in many forms and can be converted from one form to another.
e: The textbook states that energy exists in many forms and is convertible.

q: Energy sources can be classified as two major sources: conventional sources and non-conventional sources.
e: This is the primary classification of energy sources given in the text.

q: Coal, petroleum, electricity, fire wood, straw, and dried dung are conventional sources.
e: These are explicitly listed as conventional energy sources in Figure 4.7.

q: Solar energy, wind energy, tidal energy, biomass energy, and energy from urban waste are non-conventional sources.
e: These are explicitly listed as non-conventional energy sources in Figure 4.7.

q: Conventional energy sources are renewable energy sources.
e: Conventional energy sources are non-renewable, while non-conventional sources are renewable.

q: Non-conventional energy sources are renewable energy sources.
e: The textbook states that non-conventional energy sources are renewable.

q: Renewable energy sources are sustainable energy sources.
e: The textbook explicitly equates renewable energy sources with sustainable energy sources.

q: A renewable energy source is generated from unlimited natural sources and is always replenished.
e: This is the exact definition of a renewable energy source provided in the text.

q: Renewable energy sources are safe to the environment.
e: The textbook states that renewable energy sources are safe to the environment.

q: The most popular renewable energy sources currently are solar energy, wind energy, hydro energy, tidal energy, geothermal energy and biomass energy.
e: This is the exact list of popular renewable energy sources provided in the textbook.

q: Sun is the primary source of energy.
e: The textbook explicitly identifies the Sun as the primary source of energy.

q: Sunlight is a clean, renewable source of energy.
e: The textbook describes sunlight as a clean and renewable source of energy.

q: Solar energy can be used to generate electricity with the help of photovoltaic technology.
e: The textbook states that photovoltaic technology is used to generate electricity from solar energy.

q: Wind is the natural movement of air across the land or sea.
e: This is the exact definition of wind provided in the textbook.

q: The tides in the sea, the flowing water in rivers or from the dams are sources of hydro energy.
e: These are explicitly listed as sources of hydro energy in the textbook.

q: Hydro energy uses flowing water to power machinery and generate electricity.
e: This is the stated function of hydro energy in the textbook.

q: Tidal energy is another form of hydro energy that uses tidal currents twice-daily to drive turbine generator.
e: This is the exact description of tidal energy provided in the textbook.

q: Tidal flow is highly unpredictable.
e: The textbook states that tidal flow is highly predictable, unlike some other hydro energy sources.

q: Geothermal energy is more readily available in areas affected by volcanism.
e: The textbook explicitly links the availability of geothermal energy to areas affected by volcanism.

q: Biomass is plant or animal material used as fuel to produce electricity or heat.
e: This is the exact definition of biomass provided in the textbook.

q: Agricultural waste, wood, charcoal or dried dung are used as biomass.
e: These are explicitly listed as examples of biomass in the textbook.

q: Biomass can be converted into other forms of energy such as methane gas, ethanol and biodiesel.
e: The textbook states that biomass can be converted into these specific forms of energy.

q: Non-renewable energy comes from sources that will run out or will not be replenished for thousands or even millions of years.
e: This is the exact definition of non-renewable energy provided in the textbook.

q: Non-renewable energy sources are finite in amount in existence.
e: The textbook states that non-renewable energy sources exist in finite amounts.

q: Four main types of non-renewable energy sources are oil, natural gas, coal and nuclear energy.
e: These are the exact four main types of non-renewable energy sources listed in the text.

q: Oil, natural gas and coal are collectively called fossil fuels.
e: The textbook explicitly groups these three sources under the term fossil fuels.

q: Fossil fuels were formed within the earth from dead plants and animals over thousands of years.
e: Fossil fuels were formed over millions of years, not thousands of years.

q: Non-renewable energy can be used for electricity, heating, manufacturing and transportation.
e: These are the exact applications of non-renewable energy listed in the textbook.

q: Nuclear energy is produced by using elements like uranium and thorium, which cannot be replenished.
e: The textbook explicitly states that uranium and thorium cannot be replenished.

q: Nuclear energy can be used to generate electricity by means of nuclear fission.
e: The textbook states that nuclear fission is the method used to generate electricity from nuclear energy.

q: In a nuclear reactor, the nuclear fuel is used to carry out sustained fission chain reaction to produce electricity at a controlled rate.
e: This is the exact description of how a nuclear reactor functions as provided in the text.

q: Coal is a non-conventional energy source.
e: Coal is classified as a conventional energy source in the textbook.

q: Solar energy is a non-renewable energy source.
e: Solar energy is classified as a renewable (non-conventional) energy source.

q: Geothermal energy is more readily available in areas affected by earthquakes.
e: Geothermal energy is more readily available in areas affected by volcanism, not specifically earthquakes.

q: Nuclear energy can be replenished easily.
e: The textbook states that elements like uranium and thorium used for nuclear energy cannot be replenished.
